approachQuestion.prompt:
Crate Partnerships

A nondecreasing read-only array weights lists integer crate weights. A partnership consists of two distinct crate positions whose weights sum to target. Each crate can belong to at most one partnership. Return the maximum number of partnerships, not the number of all qualifying index pairs.

Constraints: 0 <= n = weights.length <= 200000; 0 <= weights[i] <= 1000000000; 0 <= target <= 2000000000. Use signed 64-bit arithmetic for sums.

Example 1: weights=[1,1,2,2,3,3], target=4 -> 3 (two 1+3 partnerships and one 2+2 partnership).
Example 2: weights=[2,2,2], target=4 -> 1.
Example 3: weights=[], target=0 -> 0.
constraints: Choose the most efficient valid approach for the entire stated input domain; accept equivalent optimal variants.

options.text: Start at both ends. If the sum is too small, advance left; if too large, decrease right. On equality count one partnership and consume both endpoints. Stop when fewer than two entries remain.
options.feedback: An impossible endpoint has no remaining partner. On equality, the two endpoint values can be matched now without reducing the maximum attainable number of partnerships.

options.text: Store all value frequencies in a balanced search tree. Process values in increasing order: for x<target-x consume the smaller of the two frequencies; for x=target-x consume half its frequency rounded down; skip x>target-x.
options.feedback: This counts disjoint uses correctly, including repeated middle values, but the ordered input makes the tree and its lookup work unnecessary.

options.text: Enumerate every index pair with the target sum and return how many such pairs exist.
options.feedback: For [2,2,2] and target 4, there are three qualifying index pairs but only one disjoint partnership.

options.text: Count each distinct pair of values with the target sum once, regardless of their frequencies.
options.feedback: For [1,1,3,3] and target 4, two partnerships are possible, but this returns one.

feedback.reason: Distinguish counting feasible pairs from maximizing disjoint uses, and justify committing a matching pair immediately.
details: Start with the smallest and largest remaining weights. Discard only the smaller endpoint if their sum is below target, or only the larger if above. On equality, add one partnership and remove both endpoints from consideration. Return the accumulated partnership count.
A too-small sum rules out the smallest endpoint with every remaining partner; a too-large sum rules out the largest. On equality consume both because a crate can belong to only one partnership.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For the fixed method revealed after question 1, choose its tight worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair. Use a word-RAM model with constant-time indexed access and signed 64-bit arithmetic. Include all temporary buffers, input copies, and call frames; exclude supplied input and returned output. n is input length. The fixed method uses no tree, hashing, copied inputs, recursion, or amortized operations. The partial alternative uses a deterministic balanced search tree, not an assumed constant-time hash table.
constraints: Analyze this fixed method regardless of your answer to question 1; choose the tightest pair.

options.text: O(n log n) time, O(1) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Every comparison consumes at least one remaining endpoint.
details: Every iteration consumes at least one endpoint and retains only indices and a count. Worst-case input requires a linear number of endpoint comparisons, giving O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

“O(n) time, O(n) auxiliary space”: This adds an input-sized buffer absent from the fixed method.
“O(n²) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: This counts repeated full scans that the fixed method does not perform.
“O(n log n) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: The fixed method does not perform sorting or independent binary searches.
